{{Short description|Heuristic for distinct words in a document}}
[[File:Heaps' Law on "War and Peace".svg|thumb|357x357px|Verification of Heaps's law on ''[[War and Peace]]'', as well as a randomly shuffled version of it. Both cases fit well to the Heaps's law with very similar exponents ''β'', but different ''K''.]]
[[Image:Heaps_law_plot.png|right|261x261px|thumb|A schematic Heaps-law plot. The x-axis represents the text size, and the y-axis represents the number of distinct vocabulary elements present in the text. Compare the values of the two axes.]]
In [[linguistics]], '''Heaps's law''' (sometimes spelled as '''Heaps' law'''), also called '''Herdan's law''', is an [[empirical law]] which describes the number of distinct words in a document (or set of documents) as a function of the document length (so called type-token relation). It can be formulated as

:<math> V_R(n) = Kn^\beta </math>

where ''V<sub>R</sub>'' is the number of distinct words in an instance text of size ''n''. ''K'' and β are free parameters determined empirically. With English [[text corpus|text corpora]], typically ''K'' is between 10 and 100, and β is between 0.4 and 0.6.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Rosillo-Rodes |first1=Pablo |last2=San Miguel |first2=Maxi |last3=Sánchez |first3=David |date=2025-07-14 |title=Entropy and type-token ratio in gigaword corpora |url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/rxxz-lk3n |journal=Physical Review Research |language=en |volume=7 |issue=3 |article-number=033054 |doi=10.1103/rxxz-lk3n |bibcode=2025PhRvR...7c3054R |issn=2643-1564}}</ref>

The law is frequently attributed to [[Harold Stanley Heaps]], but was originally discovered by {{harvs|first=Gustav|last=Herdan|year=1960|txt}}.<ref>{{harvtxt|Egghe|2007}}: "Herdan's law in linguistics and Heaps' law in information retrieval are different formulations of the same phenomenon".</ref> Under mild assumptions, the Herdan–Heaps law is asymptotically equivalent to [[Zipf's law]] concerning the frequencies of individual words within a text.<ref>{{harvtxt|Kornai|1999}}; {{harvtxt|Baeza-Yates|Navarro|2000}}; {{harvtxt|van Leijenhorst|van der Weide|2005}}.</ref> This is a consequence of the fact that the type-token relation (in general) of a homogenous text can be derived from the distribution of its types.<ref>{{harvtxt|Milička|2009}}</ref>

Empirically, Heaps's law is preserved even when the document is randomly shuffled,<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last1=Sano |first1=Yukie |last2=Takayasu |first2=Hideki |last3=Takayasu |first3=Misako |date=2012 |title=Zipf's Law and Heaps' Law Can Predict the Size of Potential Words |journal=Progress of Theoretical Physics Supplement |language=en |volume=194 |pages=202–209 |doi=10.1143/PTPS.194.202 |bibcode=2012PThPS.194..202S |issn=0375-9687|doi-access=free }}</ref> meaning that it does not depend on the ordering of words, but only the frequency of words.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Najafi |first1=Elham |last2=Darooneh |first2=Amir H. |date=2015-06-19 |editor-last=Esteban |editor-first=Francisco J. |title=The Fractal Patterns of Words in a Text: A Method for Automatic Keyword Extraction |journal=PLOS ONE |language=en |volume=10 |issue=6 |article-number=e0130617 |doi=10.1371/journal.pone.0130617 |issn=1932-6203 |pmc=4474631 |pmid=26091207 |bibcode=2015PLoSO..1030617N |doi-access=free }}</ref> This is used as evidence for deriving Heaps's law from Zipf's law.<ref name=":0" />

Heaps's law means that as more instance text is gathered, there will be diminishing returns in terms of discovery of the full vocabulary from which the distinct terms are drawn.

Deviations from Heaps's law, as typically observed in English text corpora, have been identified in corpora generated with large language models.<ref>{{cite conference | last1 = Lai | first1 = Uyen | last2 = Randhawa | first2 = Gurjit | last3 = Sheridan | first3 = Paul | title = Heaps' Law in GPT-Neo Large Language Model Emulated Corpora | book-title = Proceedings of the Tenth International Workshop on Evaluating Information Access (EVIA 2023), a Satellite Workshop of the NTCIR-17 Conference | place = Tokyo, Japan | pages = 20–23 | doi = 10.20736/0002001352 | date = 2023-12-12 | url = https://research.nii.ac.jp/ntcir/workshop/OnlineProceedings17/EVIA/abstract_evia.html#EVIA03}}</ref>

Heaps's law also applies to situations in which the "vocabulary" is just some set of distinct types which are attributes of some collection of objects. For example, the objects could be people, and the types could be country of origin of the person. If persons are selected randomly (that is, we are not selecting based on country of origin), then Heaps's law says we will quickly have representatives from most countries (in proportion to their population) but it will become increasingly difficult to cover the entire set of countries by continuing this method of sampling.
Heaps's law has been observed also in single-cell [[transcriptomes]]<ref>{{Cite journal| biorxiv = 10.1101/2021.06.16.448706| pages = 2021–06.16.448706| last1 = Lazzardi| first1 = Silvia| last2 = Valle| first2 = Filippo| last3 = Mazzolini| first3 = Andrea| last4 = Scialdone| first4 = Antonio| last5 = Caselle| first5 = Michele| last6 = Osella| first6 = Matteo| title = Emergent statistical laws in single-cell transcriptomic data| journal = Physical Review E| date = 2023| volume = 107| issue = 4| article-number = 044403| doi = 10.1103/PhysRevE.107.044403| pmid = 37198814}}</ref> considering [[genes]] as the distinct objects in the "vocabulary".
